summaries.summary: One night, the child made a snowman and went inside to sleep. In the morning, more snow had fallen. The child went out to shovel, but the walks were already clear. No one else was outside except the snowman. The child wondered if the snowman had been part of a snowman shoveling crew. The story then shows many jobs snowmen can do. A dentist fixes a snowman’s smile with coal bits, a brush, and polish. A snow mechanic straightens a crooked sled. A grocer fills shelves with frozen peas, frosty flakes, and ice cream. Snow children visit the snow pet store, and the baker makes frosted buns, cake, and ice cold rolls. Teachers help snow children count snowflakes and spell words. Snow magicians do tricks, and firefighters help a snow cat. A librarian reads stories, the pizza man brings frozen pizza, and factory workers make toys. At the end, the child thinks the snowman may really have shoveled snow after all.

video_title: Stellaluna | Read Aloud for Kids! | Bedtime Stories

summaries.summary: Stellaluna was a baby fruit bat who lived with her mother in a warm forest. One night an owl attacked the bats. Mother bat was hurt, and baby Stellaluna fell into the dark forest. She held on to a twig, but by morning she fell again and landed in a bird nest. Three baby birds lived there: Flap, Flitter, and Pip. Their mama fed them bugs, and Stellaluna was very hungry, so she ate bugs too. She learned to stay awake in the day and sleep at night, but she still liked to hang by her feet. The bird mama was upset and told Stellaluna to obey the rules. Later, Stellaluna learned to fly with the birds, but she got lost in the dark. Then she met other bats and found her own mother. The bats showed her fruit, and Stellaluna was happy. At last, Stellaluna brought the birds to meet the bats, and they all stayed friends even though they were different.

In a forest far away, a mother fruit bat had a baby named Stellaluna. She carried Stellaluna when she flew out to find food. One night an owl chased the bats. Mother bat tried to escape, but the owl struck again and Stellaluna fell far down into the trees. She caught a small twig, then fell again at daybreak and landed in a nest with three baby birds. The birds were named Flap, Flitter, and Pip. Their mother brought them bugs to eat. Stellaluna was hungry, so she ate bugs too, and she learned to live like the birds. She stayed awake in the day, slept at night, and obeyed the bird mama’s rules. When the babies grew, they learned to fly. Stellaluna flew too, but she got lost after dark. She met her bat family, who welcomed her back and showed her fruit. Later she brought Pip, Flitter, and Flap to meet the bats. The birds could not fly in the dark, but Stellaluna saved them. In the end, the birds and bats knew they were different, but they were still friends.

She stayed up in the daytime and slept at night, but she still wanted to hang by her feet. The bird mama made her promise to follow the house rules. When the nest babies grew, they learned to fly. Her mother hugged her and showed her fruit. Stellaluna later visited the birds and took them to meet the bats. The birds could not see in the dark, and Stellaluna could, so she helped them. At the end, the friends sat together and knew they were alike in some ways and different in others.

video_title: 🎃From Seed to Pumpkin 🎃| Read Aloud for Kids! | Fall Books for Kids!

summaries.summary: A farmer plants hundreds of pumpkin seeds when spring winds warm the earth. The seeds are covered with dark, moist soil. Inside the soil, the seeds crack open and grow into baby pumpkin plants. Roots grow down and stems grow up. Green shoots soon poke through the earth and become seedlings. summaries.summary: One day it rained hearts, and Cornelia Augusta caught one heart, then another, and many more. She thought it must be close to Valentine's Day, so she began making valentines. Pinkalicious renamed him Flutterbye, and he flew out into the blue sky.

You can see, smell, and hear that spring is here. Then it is time to wait for summer.

summaries.summary: In a pasture in Spain, a little bull named Ferdinand lived with other young bulls. They liked to run, jump, and butt their heads, but Ferdinand liked flowers. He sat under a cork tree and smelled them. His mother asked him to play, but Ferdinand stayed in his favorite place, and she let him. When Ferdinand grew into a big bull, the other bulls kept fighting and wanted to go to the bull fights in Madrid. Ferdinand still wanted only to sit quietly. One day, five men came to choose a bull for Madrid. The other bulls tried hard to look fierce. Ferdinand went to his cork tree, but he sat on a bumblebee. The bee stung him, and he jumped and snorted. The men thought he was the fiercest bull and took him away in a cart. In Madrid, the banderillos, picadores, and matador came into the ring. Ferdinand did not fight. He sat down and smelled the flowers in the ladies’ hair. The men were angry, and they sent him home again.

Mr. Small toots the horn and scares the ducks and chickens. A small dog follows, but it is soon left far behind because the little Auto goes fast. The car passes a horse and buggy, goes uphill and downhill, and comes to town. Mr. Small drives on the right side of the street, waits at the stop go sign, and stops at a filling station to buy 5 gallons of gas.

Johnny’s parents were surprised, and the bear stayed with them. He drank milk from the cows, ate mash meant for the chickens, ate apples from the orchard, and liked pancakes on Sunday morning. Johnny took him west, then east, then south on a boat, but the bear always came back. At last, Johnny and his father went north and found a trap. The bear ran into it, and the men said it was for the city zoo. Johnny agreed to visit and bring maple sugar.

summaries.summary: In a meadow near an old stone wall, a family of field mice lived in a home by the barn and granary. The farmers had moved away, so the barn was empty and winter was coming. The mice worked day and night to gather corn, nuts, wheat, and straw. Frederick did not carry food like the others. When they asked why, he said he was gathering sun rays for the cold winter days. When they asked again, he said he was gathering colors because winter is gray. When they thought he was dreaming, he said he was gathering words because winter days are long. When snow came, the mice stayed in their stone hideout. At first they had food and told stories, but soon the food was gone and it was cold and quiet. Then Frederick shared his sun rays, colors, and words. His story made the mice feel warm and happy. They clapped and said, “You are Frederick!”

I measure things.” The robin asked the inchworm to measure his tail. The inchworm counted, “One, two, three, four, five inches.” The robin was pleased and said his tail was five inches long. Then the robin flew with the inchworm to measure other birds. They measured the canary’s beak, the heron’s legs, the pheasant’s tail, and even the whole hummingbird. One morning, the nightingale met the inchworm and told him to measure her song. The inchworm said he could measure things, not songs. The nightingale said she would eat him for breakfast if he did not try. So the inchworm began to measure while the nightingale sang. He counted and counted until the song was very, very long and hard to measure. At the end, the inchworm forgot what he was doing and thanked the nightingale.

One morning the tadpole woke up with two little legs and said, “Look, I am a frog!” The minnow said he could not be a frog because he had been a little fish the night before. They argued, and the tadpole said, “Frogs are frogs and fish is fish and that’s that.” In the weeks after that, the tadpole grew front legs, his tail got smaller, and he changed into a real frog. He climbed out of the water and onto the bank. The minnow grew into a full fish and waited. Later, the frog came back and told him about birds, cows, and people. The fish kept thinking about these things and finally jumped out of the pond to see them. But he could not breathe in the grass and cried for help. The frog saw him, pushed him back into the pond, and the fish breathed deeply and felt better in the water.

They raced through the forest, and the pine cone bounced and flew away. It hit a sleeping bear’s nose, then kept moving until it fell near the water. A bird swept down and carried the pine cone away. Cyril and Bruce were upset, and they were in danger near the edge. Cyril grabbed a branch and pulled Bruce to safety. After that, Bruce saw how greedy he had been. The two squirrels said sorry, laughed, and became friends who shared and worked together.

Poco kept playing until the wolf ate the rabbit. Poco stopped and told the wolf, “No more eating band members or you’re out the band.” The wolf said sorry. After that, they played music again, and many animals joined the group. The crowd followed Poco all the way to her home. The music got louder and carried her parents off into the woods. Her father said he thought Poco was pretty good, and her mother could not hear him because she was busy with her book.

summaries.summary: A long time ago, many people believed black people and white people should be kept apart. This was called segregation. Black children and white children could not always go to the same schools. The United States government said this was wrong and said children should be able to go to any school they wanted. Ruby Bridges was a little girl who first went to kindergarten at a school for black children. She liked her teacher and friends, but the William Franz Elementary School was closer to her home. The government said Ruby should be allowed to go there. In 1961, Ruby’s mother took her to the Franz school, and marshalls came to keep them safe. Some people stood outside and yelled at her, and many parents took their children home. Ruby stayed with her teacher, Mrs. Henry, and learned math and reading. After many months, other children came back, and Ruby finally had friends to play with. Later, many people read about Ruby, and artists and writers made her story famous. When Ruby grew up, she visited schools and told children to be kind to each other.

summaries.summary: Wilma Rudolph lived in Clarksville, Tennessee, with her large family. She loved to run, laugh, and play, but before she was five, she became very sick. Doctors found that she had scarlet fever and polio, and people said she might never walk again. Wilma could only move by hopping on one foot. Her mother took her by bus to a hospital in Nashville, where doctors and nurses helped her do exercises. At home, Wilma kept practicing, even when it hurt. She was sad when her school would not let her attend because she could not walk. Later, she got a steel brace and returned to school, where other children made fun of her. Wilma kept working hard. One Sunday at church, she took off her brace and walked down the aisle by herself. After that, she practiced more, and when she was 12, she no longer needed the brace. She then played basketball, won many games, and later went to the Olympics in Rome. There she won three gold medals and became known as the fastest woman in the world.

Wilma Rudolph was one of 19 children in Clarksville, Tennessee. She was active and always wanted to run, but as a little girl she got very sick many times. When she was almost five, her left leg twisted inward. A doctor said she had polio, and people in town believed she would never walk again. Wilma did not give up. She hopped around the house and went to church that way. Twice a week, her mother took her on a long bus ride to Nashville so Wilma could get treatment at a hospital for Black patients. Wilma practiced her exercises at home, even though she could not go to school at first. After she got a heavy brace, she returned to school, but other children teased her. She watched basketball closely, learned the game, and kept strengthening her legs. One Sunday at church, she removed her brace and walked down the aisle. Later, she stopped using the brace for good, played basketball in high school, earned a scholarship to Tennessee State University, and then competed in the 1960 Olympics. In Rome, she won the 100 meter dash, the 200 meter dash, and the 400 meter relay.

summaries.summary: Rosa Parks grew up in America at a time when black people were treated unfairly. As a child, she was small and often sick, but she learned to stand up for herself. When she was 11, a boy on rollerskates shoved her, and she pushed him back. His mother yelled because Rosa was black, but Rosa stayed calm and told the truth. At school, Rosa saw that black children had a small old wooden school with one room, few books, and only five months of school. White children had a new brick school with many books, a playground, and nine months of school. Black children had to walk, while white children rode buses. Later, Rosa worked with the NAACP and fought for fair laws. She would not use separate water fountains or elevators. Then, at age 42, she was told to give up her bus seat. She stayed seated, was arrested, and her action helped start the Montgomery bus boycott. After 381 days, the bus rules changed, and people could no longer be separated by skin color.

Rosa Parks grew up when black people and white people were kept apart by unfair laws. She was small for her age and got sick often, but she was taught to respect herself. At 11, a boy on rollerskates shoved her. Rosa pushed him back, and even when his mother got angry, Rosa calmly explained what had happened. Rosa also saw unfairness at school. Black children had a small wooden school with one teacher, few books, and only five months of school. White children had a brick school with new desks, more books, and a playground, and they went to school longer. Black children walked, while white children rode buses. As Rosa got older, she worked with the NAACP and helped fight for fair laws. On a bus in Montgomery, Alabama, the driver told her to give up her seat for a white man. Rosa did not move, was arrested, and her action helped start the Montgomery bus boycott. After 381 days, the bus system changed its rules.

summaries.summary: Michael has just moved with his family to Falconer Road. video_title: The Sour Grape | kids storytime, classroom read aloud, jory john, pete oswald, SEL lesson for kids

summaries.summary:
The story is about a grape girl who starts out sweet but becomes sour. When she was young, she lived in a big grape bunch on a vine with many other grapes. They were kind to each other, and her grandparents visited on weekends to teach lessons about being kind, forgiving, considerate, and grateful. For a while, she listened and stayed sweet.

Later, she planned a birthday party for a long time. She sent invitations, and the party was supposed to have a ferris wheel, a magician, hay rides, snacks, and fireworks at sundown. She waited for the guests, but nobody came. Because of that, she became bitter and began holding grudges against a banana, an orange, and a lime. She kept acting this way until she went to meet Lenny, her sour friend. On the way, she hurt her knee, got a flat tire, missed the bus, and got off at the wrong stop. By the time she reached the park, Lenny was furious that she was late and would not listen. Seeing him made her think about her own behavior. Then she found the invitation and learned she had written May 31st instead of May 21st. She understood the mistake was hers. After that, she tried to talk, listen, forgive, and let go of her grudges.

Seeing the sky and park made her think differently, and she later found out she had written the wrong birthday date on the invitation. She realized the party had been her mistake. After that, she began talking things out, letting go of grudges, and being kinder again.

summaries.summary: Mr. Watson and Mrs. Watson live with their pig, Mercy, at 54 Dearoo Drive. One Saturday, Mr. Watson reads about a movie at the Beu called When Pigs Fly. Mrs. Watson likes the title, and Mercy wakes up when she hears about real butter on bottomless buckets of popcorn. The Watsons decide to go to the movie. Baby Lincoln, Eugene Lincoln, Stella, and Frank join them in the Watson convertible. At the Beu, ticket seller Beatus Leah Pon is surprised to see Mercy in the back seat, but she lets them in. Inside, Mercy smells butter and follows it. She runs to many cars and eats hot buttered popcorn from people’s buckets. People scream, laugh, and faint. Mr. and Mrs. Watson worry because Mercy is missing. Animal control officer Francine Pallet tries to catch Mercy, and officer Tomalo comes to help after hearing the trouble. Mercy keeps running until firemen Ned and Lorenzo arrive. They offer her toast with butter, and Mercy stops. Everyone ends up together eating toast, and the day ends happily.

Jabari built a ramp and put the machine on top, but it went up and crashed down. He thought it might be too heavy. Jabari kept working. He gathered his tools, cleaned his space, and made new plans. He built a bigger ramp and tried again, but the machine still did not work. His dad said he looked upset and told him to take a deep breath and try again. Jabari calmed down and said he would try again with his partner. Together they thought of better wings. They cut, glued, shaped, and tied the parts. Jabari found the launch spot, held the machine up, and let it go. It flew all the way across the yard. Jabari and his dad said they did it, and Jabari said the next project would be a rocket to Jupiter.

video_title: How I Spent My Summer Vacation Book | read aloud, narrative writing, imagination, visualization

summaries.summary: When summer began, Wallace went west because his parents wanted him to rest and calm his wild imagination. He rode a westbound train to visit Aunt Fern, but a group of Cowboys captured him and took him to their Cow Camp instead. The cattle boss said they needed a new Cowboy because the old one had quit, and Wallace agreed to help. He wrote Aunt Fern a note to tell her where he was. That night he got new clothes and looked like a Wrangler, but he learned that being a cowboy meant more than wearing boots and a hat. Over the next days, he learned roping, riding, and making fire with sticks. Soon everyone said Wallace was a first-rate cowhand. When the roundup was over, Aunt Fern invited him and the Cowboys to a barbecue. While they were eating, the cattle began to stamp and a stampede started. Wallace found a tablecloth on the ground and spun it like a lasso. The cattle ran away, and the Cowboys cheered and called him a true Buckaroo.

Wallace’s parents sent him west for the summer because they thought he needed a rest. He was supposed to visit Aunt Fern, but on the train he was captured by rough, loud Cowboys and taken to their Cow Camp. The cattle boss told him they needed a new Cowboy, since the old one had quit. Wallace said yes and wrote Aunt Fern a message so she would know he was safe. The Cowboys gave him cowboy clothes, and he soon looked like a Wrangler. Then he learned many cowboy skills, including riding, roping, and making fire with sticks. After a while, people everywhere said Wallace was a first-rate cowhand. When the roundup ended, Aunt Fern invited Wallace and the Cowboys to a barbecue at her house. During the meal, the cattle became frightened and a stampede began. Wallace grabbed a tablecloth from the ground and spun it around in a new way. The cattle turned away, the stampede stopped, and everyone cheered for Wallace.

video_title: Chrysanthemum Read Aloud | classic classroom story, back to school, self love, acceptance, teasing

summaries.summary: At the start of the story, Chrysanthemum is born and her parents choose her name with care. They call her Chrysanthemum and say it is perfect. As she grows, Chrysanthemum loves her name very much. She likes saying it, hearing it, and writing it. When school begins, she is excited, but the children laugh at her name during roll call. They say it is too long and that she is named after a flower. Chrysanthemum feels sad and thinks her name is not good anymore. Her parents comfort her at home and tell her again that her name is wonderful. The next day, the teasing starts again at school, and Chrysanthemum feels even more unhappy. Later, Mrs. Twinkle, the music teacher, says her own name is Delphinium Twinkle and that she thinks Chrysanthemum is a perfect name. Chrysanthemum feels proud again. The class musical is a success, and Mrs. Twinkle later names her baby girl Chrysanthemum.

summaries.summary: Chrysanthemum was born to parents who thought she was perfect, and they gave her the name Chrysanthemum because they wanted it to match how special she was. As she grew, Chrysanthemum loved her name. She liked hearing it from her mother and father, seeing it written on envelopes and birthday cake, and writing it herself. When she started school, she was excited at first, but the other children giggled when Mrs. Chud read her name. Joe said it was too long, Rita said it barely fit on her name tag, and Victoria said it was a flower name and that she would change it if it were hers. Chrysanthemum went home upset, and her parents told her her name was beautiful and perfect. The next day, the teasing continued, and Victoria said Chrysanthemum looked like a flower. Chrysanthemum had a bad dream about being picked apart like a flower. Later, Mrs. Twinkle, the music teacher, explained that her own name was Delphinium Twinkle and that she had been thinking of Chrysanthemum as a name for her baby. Hearing this made Chrysanthemum feel proud again. In the end, the class musical was a success, and Mrs. Twinkle later named her baby girl Chrysanthemum.

summaries.summary: Mommy and Poppy spend many days trying to get Lola to eat shrimp. They tell her shrimp will help her feathers, eyes, and wings. But Lola keeps leaving when they are not looking. She doddles and sidesteps away from the water and finds other foods to eat. She eats creamy avocado under berry trees, sweet Pepino melons among evergreen shrubs, and juicy dragon fruits near a pebble path and moonbeam flowers. After each meal, Mommy or Poppy asks what she ate, and Lola tells them. Mommy and Poppy keep eating shrimp themselves and say it tastes yummy. Lola says shrimp are yucky because she has never tried them. At the end, Mommy asks her to eat just one bite. Lola says she could try shrimp. She goes to the shoreline, dips her beak into the water, and catches one tiny shrimp. Lola eats it and says she loves yummy shrimp. Mommy and Poppy say Lola did eat shrimp.

They are bigger and have noses that are not flat. Vervet monkeys are one kind of Old World monkey. Monkey mothers stay close to their babies, and the babies learn from them. summaries.summary: Nikki wanted new mittens made of wool as white as snow. His grandmother Baba did not want to make white mittens at first because she said they could be lost in the snow. Nikki wanted them, so Baba made them. She told him she would look to see if he was safe and sound when he came home, and then she would look to see if he still had his Snow White mittens. Nikki went outside, and soon one mitten dropped in the snow. A mole found it and crawled inside. Then a snowshoe rabbit came by and squeezed in too. A hedgehog, an owl, a badger, a fox, and a great bear all came to live in the mitten as well. The mitten stretched, but Baba's knitting held. Then a tiny mouse climbed in. The mouse tickled the bear, and the bear sneezed. The sneeze sent the mitten and the animals flying apart. Nikki saw the mitten in the sky and ran to get it. When he got home, Baba saw that he was safe and still had his mittens.

Nikki went out, and one mitten fell into the snow. A mole found the mitten and went inside because it was warm and cozy. A snowshoe rabbit came next and joined the mole. In the end, Baba looked out and saw that Nikki was home safe and still had his Snow White mittens.

summaries.summary: At the top of a hill, just outside town, there was a house with woods behind it and a brook nearby. When Cora was young, she looked at the house and dreamed of making it into a world wonder. She grew up and became a world-famous architect. She built a stadium, a museum, schools, factories, and monuments, but she never thought any of them were wonderful enough. When she got older, she came home and found the house empty and for sale. She bought it, fixed it up, painted the walls, repaired the fence, planted seeds, and got chickens. Then she met children in the woods who were building a fort. Cora helped them, and later the townspeople asked her to help with their projects too. Together they built many things. In the end, Cora saw that the house and the memories in it were wonderful just as they were.

Cora lived near a house on a hill outside town. As a child, she imagined turning it into something special, like a bed-and-breakfast or an amusement park. When she grew up, she became a famous architect and made many big buildings, including a stadium and a museum. People called them world wonders, but Cora always wanted something more. After many years of work, she became tired and returned home. The house was empty, so she bought it and began fixing it up. She painted, repaired, planted, and kept chickens. While walking in the woods, she found children building a fort from logs and branches. They asked her to help, and she worked with them for weeks. The townspeople came to see the fort, and after that they asked Cora to help them too. Cora worked with the town on desks, birdhouses, bookshelves, bunk beds, a train set, and a scooter. She then realized the house was already wonderful.

summaries.summary: The Bear family visits the Bear Country Space Center, where rockets blast off into outer space. A guide shows them a launchpad and says it is where rockets are fueled. Papa looks around and sees one big red button. He wonders what it does and pushes it. Right away, the rocket roars and shakes. Then the guide, who is also a rocket pilot, takes over the rocket and turns it around. He flies it back to Earth and makes a perfect landing at the space center. Everyone cheers. Papa says he only wanted to see what the button was for, and then he kisses the ground and says he wants no more space travel.

The mayor called everyone in Whoville to shout. Their voices were still not enough until Jojo made one more sound. Then the Whos were heard, and Horton saved them.

video_title: Snowflake Bentley

summaries.summary: Wilson Bentley, known as Willie, was born in Vermont where winter snow was common. As a boy, he loved watching snowflakes fall and wished he could save their beauty. His mother taught him at home, and when she gave him a microscope, he used it to study snow crystals. He discovered that the crystals had six branches and that no two were the same. Willie first tried to draw the snowflakes, but they melted before he could finish. Then he learned about a camera that could take close pictures. His parents spent their savings to buy it, and Willie worked hard even when the first photographs failed. After many tries, he found a way to photograph snowflakes by using a small lens opening and long exposure. He also learned how to make the crystals show more clearly. Willie kept working through many winters, making pictures, giving talks, and sharing them with children, adults, and schools. He became famous as the snowflake man, published Snow Crystals, and later died after walking home in a blizzard and becoming ill with pneumonia.

His teacher, Miss Kirby, stomped around and shouted, “Move it or lose it!” and “Settle down!” She said children who threw paper airplanes in class would miss recess. Bobby spent his free time in the park trying to forget his teacher troubles. One Saturday morning, while he was walking to his favorite spot, Bobby found Miss Kirby there. He wanted to run away, but he stayed. They talked in a careful way, and Bobby said hello and told her he liked her enormous hat. Then a gust of wind blew the hat away, and Miss Kirby asked Bobby to catch it. Bobby grabbed the hat and gave it back. After that, they watched ducks and quacked with them. Bobby showed Miss Kirby his favorite spot in the park, and she liked it. Bobby then flew his paper airplane, and it flew very far. By lunchtime, Bobby and Miss Kirby were happy and said goodbye. At school later, Miss Kirby still stomped and roared, but Bobby had seen her outside school too.

Instead, he spoke to her, said hello, and noticed her enormous hat. Miss Kirby said the hat came from her granny. Then the wind blew, and the hat started to get away. Bobby caught it and gave it back to her. Miss Kirby thanked him. After that, ducks came by, and Bobby and Miss Kirby quacked with them. Bobby showed her his favorite place in the park, and she said to be careful. Miss Kirby then had an idea. Bobby threw his paper airplane into the sky, and it flew and flew and flew. They both said it was the greatest paper airplane flight ever. At lunch, they said goodbye. When Bobby saw Miss Kirby back at school, she still stomped and roared, but Bobby knew her in a new way.

He also wants them to know when to say thank you, and when to say excuse me. Mr. Rabbit says otters should be honest and keep their promises. He says they should be considerate by listening, asking before borrowing, not littering, being patient, helping others, and being on time. He says otters should be kind and cooperate with others. He also wants them to play fair, share, not tease, and apologize when they do something wrong. At the end, Mr. Rabbit says that this is how he would like otters to treat him, and that the rule is simple.

video_title: The Secret Life Of Squirrels: Back To School

summaries.summary: Rosie has a busy day before school begins. She feels excited and a little nervous because her students will arrive tomorrow. Mr. Peanuts helps her get ready. First, they go shopping for school supplies. Rosie picks notebooks, paper, paints, and crayons. Then they go to the classroom. Mr. Peanuts unpacks books for the library, and Rosie hangs a banner and posts the class rules. Mr. Peanuts helps outside with sports equipment for recess and gym. Next, Rosie asks him to help in the art corner, but he knocks over a purple paint can. Rosie says not to worry and keeps paper towels nearby. They eat lunch, and after that Mr. Peanuts practices the bus route. Rosie tidies the community garden, stores first aid supplies in the closet, talks to Miss Chattery, checks the microphone, and finishes her lesson plan. At the end, Rosie checks her list and sees that all the work is done for the first day of school.

At the end, they look at another animal and argue again, saying it is an ant eater or a brachiosaurus.

video_title: Sophie's Squash

summaries.summary:
One fall day, Sophie picked a squash at the farmer's market. She wanted to keep it, not eat it. Sophie gave the squash a face, wrapped it in a blanket, and named her Bernice. She rocked Bernice to sleep and took her to story time, the farmer's market, and the garden. Sophie gave Bernice a bottle, a hug, and a kiss.

Sophie's mother said Bernice was not a friend and talked about baking her with marshmallows. Sophie's father wanted Sophie to pick a toy, but Sophie said she had everything she needed. Later, her parents wanted to donate Bernice to the food pantry. At the library, some kids pointed at Bernice, and Sophie said Bernice should not stay home. When winter came, Bernice got softer. Sophie asked a farmer how squash stay healthy, and he said they need fresh air, good clean dirt, and a little love. Sophie put Bernice in the garden and left her there under the snow. In winter, her father brought home Ace, a fish. When spring came, Sophie found a green sprout. In summer, Bernice grew two tiny squash named Bonnie and Baxter.

summaries.summary: One bright fall day, Sophie picked a squash at the farmer’s market and decided it was her friend. She named it Bernice, drew a face on it with markers, wrapped it in a blanket, and rocked it to sleep. When her parents wanted to cook it, Sophie said Bernice was not for supper. Bernice went everywhere with Sophie, including the library and the garden, and Sophie treated her like a pet. Her parents tried to explain that Bernice was a squash and would get mushy if they did not eat her, but Sophie would not agree. As winter came, Bernice became softer. Sophie learned from a farmer that squash need fresh air, good dirt, and a little love, so she planted Bernice in the garden and covered her with soft soil. After winter, a green sprout appeared. In summer, Bernice grew into two tiny squash named Bonnie and Baxter, and Sophie loved them too.

After the snow melted, Sophie found a small green sprout. By summer, Bernice had grown two tiny squash, Bonnie and Baxter, and Sophie ate lunch with them and Ace every day.

video_title: Wonders Grade 5- One Hen

summaries.summary: Cojo lives in a village in the Ashanti region of Ghana with his mother. After his father dies, Cojo stops going to school and helps his mother gather firewood to sell. Their village has a special money plan. Each family saves a little, and one family borrows the savings to start something important. Cojo’s mother uses her loan to buy a cart for firewood. Cojo asks for the leftover coins and buys a brown hen with a bright red comb. He takes care of the hen, checks for eggs, and soon she lays many. Cojo and his mother eat some eggs and sell the rest at the market. With the egg money, Cojo buys more hens, then goes back to school. He studies hard, earns a scholarship, and later goes to agricultural college. After college, he borrows money from a bank and starts a big poultry farm. His farm grows, helps many people, and Cojo’s family becomes stronger too.

Cojo is tired and hungry when he brings firewood home to his mother. He smells her Fufu cooking and walks faster. Their family has little money, but the village shares savings so each family can borrow in turn. First the Achampong family borrows money to buy fruit. Then the Duodu family borrows money to buy a sewing machine. When it is Cojo’s mother’s turn, she buys a cart for firewood. Cojo uses the leftover money to buy a brown hen from a farmer in another village. He carries the hen home in a basket and keeps her safe beside his bed. Soon the hen lays eggs. Cojo sells eggs at market and saves the money. After two months he buys another hen. After six months he buys a third hen. Later he has 25 hens. He uses his egg money to return to school, then studies more at agricultural college. After college he gets a bank loan, buys 900 hens, and starts a poultry farm that grows very large.

Cojo and his mother live in a mud house with a garden in Ghana. They do not have much money or much food. Their village has 20 families, and each family saves money so another family can borrow it. Cojo’s mother borrows first and buys a cart. Cojo then takes the leftover coins and walks two hours to a chicken farm. He looks at many hens until he sees a plump brown hen with a bright red comb. He buys her and takes her home in a wicker basket. Cojo makes a nest for her and checks for eggs every day. At last he finds one, and soon she lays five eggs in the first week. Cojo and his mother eat some and sell the others at the market. He saves the money, buys more hens, and later pays for school again. He learns reading, writing, math, farming, and more. After college he gets a bigger loan, builds a farm, and buys 900 hens. The farm grows, and many people work there and earn wages.

video_title: Wonders Grade 5 Weslandia

summaries.summary:
Wesley lived in a town where he felt different from everyone else. He did not like pizza or soda, and he thought professional football was stupid. He would not shave half his head like the other boys, even when his father offered him five dollars. He had no friends and was often chased by tormentors. Every day his mother asked what he learned at school. One day Wesley realized he could use what he learned to make a summer project. He decided to grow his own food crop and found his own civilization.

He turned over a patch of ground in his yard, and after a windy night, plants began to grow. The plant made fruit, roots, leaves, bark, and fibers that Wesley used for food, drink, clothes, oil, and tools. He made a hat, a robe, a sundial, new games, and even a new language. He named his land Westlandia. By the end of summer, Wesley had a whole civilization, and when he went back to school in September, he had no shortage of friends.

Wesley was not like the other children in his town. He disliked the same foods, sports, and hairstyles that everyone else liked. His parents talked about him, and he had many tormentors but no friends. At school, Wesley learned that seeds can travel far in the wind and that every civilization has a staple food crop. When his mother said he should find a good summer project, Wesley had an idea. He decided to grow his own crop and build his own civilization.

He dug up a place in his yard. Soon, after a wind from the west, seeds were planted there. In five days, strange seedlings grew. Wesley’s plant was not like tomatoes, beans, or brussels sprouts. It made yellow fruit that turned magenta, and the fruit tasted like many sweet foods. Wesley ate it for breakfast, drank its juice, and cooked the tubers. He used the bark, stalk, seeds, and oil to make a hat, robe, lotion, and even games. He named his land Westlandia, created a language, wrote its history, and returned to school with friends.

The fruit changed color, and the inside tasted like peach, strawberry, and pumpkin pie. He used the plant for meals, drinks, clothing, sun protection, and mosquito repellent. He also made games, a new count based on eight, and a new language. He called his land Westlandia. In September he went back to school, and he had many friends.

summaries.summary: Tai Singh was born in the mountains near Virginia City, Nevada. He grew up loving the Sierra and learned to write in English and Chinese. As a Chinese American, life was hard, but Tai Singh made big plans. He became a trail cook and worked for map makers in the mountains. In 1915, Stephen Mather hired him to cook for a camping trip with important guests. Tai Singh planned meals for many days and worked with an assistant named Eugene. Each morning they woke early, made the fire, cooked breakfast, packed lunch, and moved camp. They washed dishes, packed the stoves, and cooked fine dinners at the next campsite. One day a mule wandered away with fancy food, so Tai Singh changed his plans and cooked a simpler meal. Later another mule fell off a cliff, and he had to make more new food. At the end, he gave the campers fortune cookies, and they remembered the trip and helped support the national parks.

Tai Singh was a frontier baby who grew up in the Sierra mountains. He learned English and Chinese, and he worked as a trail cook because he loved the mountains. His meals were so good that Stephen Mather chose him for a special camping trip in 1915. Mather wanted guests to see America’s wild places, so he brought writers, congress members, and other important people into the mountains. Tai Singh planned breakfast, lunch, and dinner for 30 people. He and Eugene woke before dawn, lit the stoves, cooked eggs and steaks, and packed food for the trail. Then they washed dishes, loaded the mule, and hurried to the next camp to make dinner. One day a mule ran away with the best food, so Tai Singh made a new menu. Another day a mule fell off a cliff, and he had to cook again with what was left. At the end, he served fortune cookies with messages inside, and later the national park service was created.

Tai Singh grew up in Nevada and loved the mountains. Even though many people treated Chinese people badly, he worked hard and became the best trail cook in California. In 1915, Stephen Mather hired him to cook for a camping trip meant to show guests the beauty of the mountains. Tai Singh planned many meals and brought flour, beef, fruit, and other food. Every morning he and Eugene woke in the dark, started the fire, cooked breakfast, and packed the camp. Then they washed dishes and moved the ovens and table to the next site. Tai Singh cooked fancy dinners there too. One day a mule walked away with the special food, so he changed his plans and made plain but tasty food. Later, another mule fell off a cliff, and the food and gear were damaged. Tai Singh still cooked a simple meal for the hungry campers. On the last night, he served fortune cookies. The campers read the messages, remembered the trip, and later helped create the national park service.

Tai Singh planned food for 30 people for 10 days. He and Eugene made fires in the cold dark morning, cooked breakfast, and packed lunches. After the others hiked away, they washed dishes and moved the camp. They cooked dinner at the next place with china plates, tablecloths, and napkins. One morning a mule carried off the fancy food, so Tai Singh made a new menu. Another day a mule fell off a cliff, and he lost much of the food and gear. He still fed everyone. At the end, he gave them fortune cookies, and the campers later helped the national park service begin.

video_title: Kamala Harris: Rooted in Justice (Literally Cultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: Eve asked questions after her mom told her about Kamala Harris. Kamala was born in Oakland, and her name meant lotus flower. Her parents, Shyamala and Donald, came from India and Jamaica and moved through Berkeley before settling in Oakland. They marched for civil rights and taught Kamala about justice and freedom. When Kamala was little, she traveled with her sister Maya to Zambia to see their grandparents. Their grandfather had fought for India’s independence, and their grandmother fought for women’s rights. After Kamala’s parents divorced, she moved to Berkeley with her mother and sister. She rode a bus to school in another part of town and learned with children from many places. Mrs. Shelton looked after her after school and gave her confidence. Kamala later moved to Montreal, then attended Howard University, ran for student office, studied law, and worked in government. She became a lawyer, senator, and presidential candidate, then ended her campaign and kept serving in the Senate.

summaries.summary: Eve comes home from first grade upset after Calvin says girls cannot be president. Her mother explains that he is wrong and begins telling Eve the true story of Kamala Harris. Kamala is born in Oakland to parents Shyamala and Donald, and her family has roots in India, Jamaica, Berkeley, and Oakland. Her parents take her to civil rights marches and teach her about peace, justice, and freedom. Kamala and her sister Maya visit their grandparents in Zambia and learn that justice runs in their family. When Kamala is seven, her parents divorce, and she moves with her mother and Maya to Berkeley. She rides a bus to school in a richer white neighborhood, where she learns with children from many backgrounds. At the Shelton House, Mrs. Regina Shelton encourages her and helps her feel confident. Kamala later studies at Howard, works hard, wins student elections, and prepares for a career in law and public service. She becomes district attorney, attorney general, and a U.S. senator, then runs for president before ending her campaign. The story ends with Eve ready to speak up for herself.

Kamala later attends Howard University, joins protests, works in government, and trains for legal work. She passes the bar after failing once, becomes a major public official, and finally announces a run for president before ending her campaign.

video_title: Kamala and Maya’s Big Idea (Literally Cultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: Kamala and Maya looked at the empty courtyard and wished for a playground. They told Mommy, and she said they should ask the landlord, the person who owns the building. Kamala wrote a letter, Maya drew a picture, and they went to ask him. The landlord said no. That night, the sisters asked the other children in the building, and the children also wanted a playground. Kamala wrote a longer letter, but the landlord said the project would cost too much. He said they could do it themselves if they wanted. The children asked their parents and neighbors for help. Most people said no, but Mr. Green said maybe he could find scrap lumber and sand. Soon the children built parts of the playground. Miss Lopez said maybe they could get an old tire for a teeter-totter. More maybes turned into yeses. They had a potluck, and later Miss Flores helped them find a slide. After a bake sale and a sidewalk sale, the slide arrived. Kamala and Maya rode it first, and the landlord said they did a good job.

Later, Miss Flores found a way to buy an old slide from Emerson Elementary. The neighbors held a potluck, a bake sale, and a sidewalk sale. At last the slide arrived, and the landlord praised the children for their work.

Mom also says, “You can do anything if you put your heart in it and try hard.” Next, the narrator finds a superhero in sister Mai, who plays with the child, stays close, and helps during sad times with an un birthday party, cake, and dancing. They help, teach, protect, and explore. At the end, the narrator grows up, becomes a lawyer and senator, works with others to help kids, and learns that heroes are kind, brave, curious, fair, and helpful. video_title: The Floating Field: How a Group of Thai Boys Built Their Own Soccer Field (Read Aloud)

summaries.summary:
Pret Hemman lived in a stilt village where boats, nets, and fish were part of daily life. Each morning he helped his father prepare the Longboat for fishing. His mother stayed in the kitchen making coffee and slicing jack fruit. Pret’s father went out to sea for groupers and prawns, but Pret wanted soccer more than fishing.

After school, Pret and his friends played on a sandbar that appeared when the tide went out. They raced from the pier, paddled a boat, planted poles, and kicked the ball until the water came back. Then the field disappeared. One month later, the boys watched the World Cup at Uncle’s coffee shop and decided to create their own team. Pret said they could build a field on the water. They gathered broken wood, empty barrels, styrofoam, and pieces from old boats and docks. They built a floating soccer field at the pier, even though some villagers laughed. After weeks of work, the field was ready, and the boys played on it every day while more and more villagers watched and cheered.

They use poles, boats, and the tide to make their game work, and they play until the water comes back and covers the field. One day they watch the World Cup at Uncle’s coffee shop and decide to make their own team. Pret suggests building a field, so the boys collect wood, barrels, styrofoam, old boat parts, and dock pieces. They build a floating field at the pier, even when villagers say it cannot be done. After weeks of work, the field is finished. The boys play there every day, and more villagers come to watch and cheer.

Pret lives in a floating village and spends his mornings helping his father with the fishing boat. His father goes out to sea for fish, while Pret goes with his friends to Uncle’s coffee shop. There they eat fried dough and talk about soccer. After school, the boys race to the sandbar, play hard, and stop when the tide rises and the field disappears. Later, when the World Cup is on television in Mexico, the boys watch games together and decide to form their own team. Pret says they can make their own field. They gather materials from broken boats, old docks, fish farms, and abandoned places, then build a platform on the water with goalposts at each end. People laugh at them at first, but the boys keep working. When the floating field is done, they play on it every day, learning to move fast on the boards and chase the ball into the water when needed. The villagers stop teasing and begin to watch.

Pret and the other boys in the village love soccer. They first play on a sandbar that appears when the tide is low. They jump into a boat, paddle out, set up poles, and play until the tide returns and ends the match. While the boys can still watch the World Cup, they gather at Uncle’s coffee shop to see teams play on the only television on the island. After one exciting game, they decide to create their own soccer team. Pret notices the hidden sandbar and says they should build their own field. The boys spend days and weeks collecting wood, barrels, styrofoam, and broken boat pieces. They carry the materials to the pier and build a floating field with goalposts. Some villagers think the idea is impossible, but the boys continue anyway. Once the field is complete, the boys play on it after school, and the villagers begin to cheer for them instead of shaking their heads.

The boys’ new floating field lets them play soccer without waiting for the tide. They build it from boards, barrels, buoys, and other scraps they find around the village. Even though some people say they are crazy, the boys keep working until the field is finished. After that, they play every day after school. The rough boards make them move carefully, and if the ball goes into the water, they chase it and keep playing. Their team becomes known as the py football club. When a tournament on the mainland is announced, the boys sign up. On the morning they leave, villagers bring them new jerseys, matching shorts, and cleats. On the mainland, the boys play on grass for the first time. They pass the ball, get open, and score a goal. Later, heavy rain floods the field during a semifinal game, and they fall behind 2 to 0. Barefoot, they fight back and score twice, but the other team scores again near the end. The py football club loses that game but finishes in third place.

Pret lives in a village on stilts, where his father fishes and his mother helps at home. Pret helps before school, then joins the boys for soccer near the pier. At first, they play on the sandbar when the tide is low and stop when the water covers it. After watching the World Cup at Uncle’s coffee shop, they decide to make their own team and build their own field. Pret suggests the idea, and the boys gather wood, old boards, barrels, styrofoam, and pieces from broken boats and docks. They build a floating soccer field at the pier, although some villagers say it will not work. When it is finished, they play there every day and the villagers start watching them. Later, the boys enter a mainland tournament and receive matching uniforms and cleats from their families. They win several games, then face a rainy semifinal. Down 2 to 0, they remove their shoes and socks and play barefoot. They score twice, but the other team scores the final goal. The py football club ends in third place and returns home proud of their field and their team.

video_title: Love in the Library (@LiterallyCultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: Tama went to the library in Minoka every day. She brushed dust from her eyes and walked past fences and guard towers. She did not like the desert, but she liked books, so she took the library job. George always waited at the door with books to return. Tama unlocked the library, and George came in. Minoka was a camp where Japanese Americans were kept. Life there was hard. It was hot, cold, muddy, and crowded, and people had no privacy. Tama did not know when she would leave. She read books and watched people come and go. The books gave her comfort, and George’s smile did too. One day, Tama felt sad and could not find the right word for her feelings. George told her, “human.” Tama smiled back and felt less alone. Then she saw that George loved her. Tama and George married, their first son was born in Minoka, and Tama wrote that the miracle was in believing in change, beauty, and hope.

summaries.summary: Tama works in the library at Minoka, a prison camp where Japanese Americans have been forced to live. She does not like the desert, the dust, or the guards, but she keeps going to work because she loves books. Every morning George waits at the library door with the books he checked out the day before. Tama and George have been in Minoka for a year, and life there is hard, with hot summers, cold winters, mud, and no privacy for families. Tama often feels fear, sadness, and loneliness, but she also finds comfort in books and in George’s big smile. When she cannot find the right word for how she feels, George tells her there is a word for it: human. Tama begins to smile again. Later she realizes that George has been coming every day because he loves her. Tama and George marry, and their first son is born in Minoka. Even in the camp, their family grows, and Tama writes that the miracle is in people who believe in change, beauty, and hope.

Tama walks through the desert to the library in Minoka, where barbed wire fences and guard towers surround the camp. She works there because she likes books, even though she does not know how to be a librarian. George is already waiting at the door each morning with the books he borrowed the day before. The story explains that Japanese Americans from the West Coast are being held in prison camps like Minoka, and that the camps are uncomfortable and unjust. Tama sees how the weather makes life harder, from heat and cold to rain and mud, and how families must share small rooms with no privacy. She keeps working and reading while days pass in the same way. Books help her feel less alone, and George’s presence does too. One day, when Tama cannot name all her feelings, George says there is a word for it: human. Tama later realizes George loves her. They marry, have a son in Minoka, and hold on to hope even while living in an unfair place.

At the start of the story, Tama goes to the library in Minoka, a camp where Japanese Americans are imprisoned during World War II. She hates the desert path, the dust, and the guards, but she keeps working because she loves books. George greets her every morning with a stack of books, and she unlocks the library for him. The story shows that life in Minoka is harsh: summers are extremely hot, winters are very cold, and rain turns the ground to mud. Families live in single rooms and have no privacy. Tama does not know when she will leave, so she spends her days in the library while people come and go depending on the weather. She feels fear and sadness, but books and George give her comfort. When she cannot find the right word for her feelings, George says it is “human.” Later Tama understands that George has been coming because he loves her. They marry, their first son is born in Minoka, and Tama writes that the miracle is in people who believe in hope and change.

George comes every day with books to return, and Tama unlocks the door for him. The story explains that people in the camps have to take whatever jobs are needed, and Tama took this job because she liked books. Minoka is shown as a place of constant discomfort. The weather is harsh in every season, and families are crowded into small rooms with no privacy. Tama does not know when she will leave, so she keeps working and watching the days pass. She feels many emotions at once and cannot name them, until George tells her there is a word for what she feels: human. Tama smiles, and later she sees that George has been in love with her all along. They marry, have a son in Minoka, and keep their family together through the injustice around them.

summaries.summary: Mom is cooking in the kitchen, and Grandma is standing near her. The family is getting ready for New Year’s, which is the child’s favorite day. Mom says, “A dragon would bring health and Fortune.” The child and friends help decorate the street with F Chun and Red Lanterns. They look for a red Dragon’s Tail and think they see a real dragon. This dragon can control water, and the child learns he is hard to catch. They try to trap him with tacos, but then they change to noodles and sticky rice. The dragon likes them and comes back for more. They try to make him sleepy, then they try gold, but nothing works. At last, they use the Dragon Dance, but the dragon is still not caught. The street is messy, so they clean up. The child tells Mom sorry and says they tried their best. Mom hugs the child, and the family watches fireworks together. The child feels lucky and says, “Better luck next year.”

video_title: Ambitious Girl (Literally Cultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: The story starts with a girl being called many names, such as too assertive, too persistent, too ambitious, too loud, too confident, and too proud. She is told that nobody else can decide who she is. She dreams about growing up in a changing world and wants to go out and do great things. Sometimes she hears words that feel heavy, but her mommy says those words can help her rise higher. The girl learns that she is valued, loved, and has purpose. She also hears from sisters, aunties, mothers, and Grandma that many women have already opened doors, and she should make room for more. Grandma says she may be the first someday, but she should not be the last. The girl says she will claim her place and show the world, “This is me.” By the end, she knows what persistent, assertive, confident, proud, and ambitious mean, and she decides to take up space, make noise, and use her voice with no fear of being “too that” or “too this.”

video_title: The Little Prince - English Reading for Beginners AUDIOBOOK (leitura guiada em para iniciantes)

summaries.summary: The story begins with a man who drew his first picture when he was six years old. He drew a snake with an elephant inside it. Grown-ups looked at it and said it was a hat, not a snake. Then he drew picture number two, but grown-ups did not care about it. He stopped drawing and later became a grown-up who flew planes all over the world. One day his plane crashed in the Sahara desert. He was alone and thirsty. The next morning he heard a small voice ask, “Draw me a sheep, please.” A boy with golden hair stood there. The man drew many sheep pictures, but the boy did not like them. At last the man drew a sheep in a box, and the little prince liked it. They talked about the prince’s small planet, his sheep, and his flower. The little prince told him about his journey, and they became close friends.

The little prince told the man about his own planet and the problems there. He said sheep eat little trees, and he wanted the sheep to eat the baobab trees before they grew too big. He also told about sunsets on his tiny planet, where he could watch many sunsets in one day. On the fifth day he asked if sheep eat flowers. He was worried because he had a special flower on his planet. The man told him he could draw a muzzle for the sheep so the flower would be safe. The little prince then told how he cared for his flower with water and a glass cover, but the flower often said hard things and told him to go away. He left his planet because he felt sad. Then he told about four small planets he visited. On each one he met a strange grown-up: a king, a man who counted stars, a lamplighter, and a writer. The writer told him to go to Earth.

On Earth, the little prince met a snake in the desert. The snake told him Earth was big and that he could help the prince go home one day. Then the prince saw a flower, walked up a mountain, and found a garden full of roses. He became sad because his own flower looked like all the other roses. After that, he met a fox under an apple tree. The fox said, “Tame me,” and explained that being tame means becoming friends. The little prince came back every day and tamed the fox. When it was time to leave, the fox told him that the heart sees what is important and that his rose was special because he had tamed her. Later, after eight days in the desert, the man and the little prince found a well and drank water. The prince asked for the sheep muzzle again. Then the prince went back to the snake. The snake bit his leg, and the prince fell quietly. The man later looked at the stars and remembered the little prince and his flower.

The story starts with the man as a child. He drew a snake with an elephant inside it, but grown-ups did not understand his picture. He made another drawing, but they were not interested. So he stopped drawing and grew up to be a plane pilot. Much later, his plane crashed in the Sahara desert. He could not fix it, and he was alone with very little water. The next morning a golden-haired boy asked him, “Draw me a sheep.” The man tried several drawings, but the little prince wanted a sheep that was small and young. At last the man drew a sheep in a box, and the prince liked it. Over the next days the prince asked many questions and spoke about his tiny planet, where baobabs had to be stopped, flowers had to be cared for, and sunsets could be watched again and again. He told about leaving his planet, visiting strange grown-ups, and coming to Earth.

On Earth, the little prince first met a snake, then a flower, then a mountain, and then a garden full of roses. He was sad because he thought his own flower was not special. After that, he met a fox. The fox asked the prince to tame him and said friends become special to each other. The little prince came back every day, and they became friends. The fox told him that important things are seen with the heart, and that the prince’s rose was special because he had cared for her. Later, the man and the little prince searched for water in the desert. They found a well and drank from it. The prince asked again for the sheep muzzle because he had to protect his flower. Then the prince said he had to go home. The snake appeared, bit him, and he fell softly on the sand. The man later said that after six years he still looked at the stars and remembered the little prince, his laugh, his flower, and the sheep.

video_title: 🪨 The Crow and the Pitcher—Aesop's Fables Short Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: A very thirsty crow looked everywhere for water. At last, she found a pitcher with some cool water inside. But the pitcher had a narrow neck, and the crow could not reach the water at the bottom. She tried, but she still could not drink. Then the crow stopped and thought. Soon she had an idea. She picked up small pebbles from the ground and dropped them into the pitcher, one by one. Each pebble made the water rise a little higher. The crow kept adding pebbles until the water came up close enough for her to drink. At last, she could reach the cool water and take a drink. After she was refreshed, the crow said, “Necessity is the mother of invention.”

A thirsty crow was searching for something to drink. She found a pitcher and peered inside. There was water at the bottom, and she was happy to see it. But the neck of the pitcher was too narrow, so she could not reach the water. The crow tried again and again, but it did not work. Then she thought carefully and cried, “Aha! I have an idea!” She found nearby pebbles and began dropping them into the pitcher. As each pebble fell in, the water rose higher. The crow kept putting in pebble after pebble. Slowly, the water moved up until it was close enough for her to drink. Finally, the thirsty crow drank the cool water and felt refreshed. Then she said, “Necessity is the mother of invention.”

One day, a very thirsty crow came to a pitcher while looking for water. She looked into the jug and saw a little water at the bottom. She wanted to drink it, but the pitcher had a narrow neck, and her beak could not reach. The crow was discouraged, but she did not stop. She paused and thought about what to do. Then she called out, “Aha!” and found a clever plan. She picked up pebbles nearby and dropped them into the pitcher. With every pebble, the water level rose a little more. The crow kept going until the water was high enough to reach. Then she drank the water and was no longer thirsty. After that, she said, “Necessity is the mother of invention.”

David plays in the snow and has snowball fights, but then he breaks a window, so Santa says he may get a lump of coal. At dinner, David does not sit right, yawns, reaches, uses the wrong fork, and keeps his elbows on the table. Santa tells him to stop and says he looks mischievous. Later, David wants to open one present early, but Santa says no and tells him to go to sleep. David thinks he will get no Christmas. In the night, David sees a lump of coal and cries, but then Santa’s note says sorry for being naughty. The next morning, David wakes up and learns it was a dream. It is Christmas, and he gets a comic book, candy cane, cookie, and a beautiful bicycle.

summaries.summary: One day, Buzz and Fly Guy were bored, so they went for a walk to find something fun to do. They played chase and cooled off in a fountain. Then they heard someone screaming. A girl was running because a fly was chasing her. Buzz told the girl not to worry because flies are pets, not pests. The girl said the fly was her pet, and her name was Fly Girl. Buzz introduced Fly Guy, and the girl introduced Fly Girl. Fly Guy and Fly Girl both showed tricks. Fly Guy ate gross things, and Fly Girl ate even grosser things. Buzz and the girl learned each other’s names: Buzz and Liz. Then Buzz asked Liz if she wanted to play on the swings, and they went to the park together. After that, Fly Guy and Fly Girl sat together and talked in fly talk. They imagined getting married and having a home, but then they remembered Buzz and Liz. At the end, Fly Guy and Fly Girl said they should just be friends.

video_title: ⏳🐱 A 35-Minute Adventure with Pete the Cat! 🎉📚

summaries.summary: Pete walks to school in his red shoes on his four furry feet. He sings, “I’m rocking in my school shoes!” At school, Pete is first in the classroom, where he sits at his desk and does not seem to listen. His teacher sends him down the hall to the library. Pete goes to the room with books and every wall. He has never been there before, but he finds a favorite book and sings, “I’m reading in my school shoes!” Then Pete goes to the lunchroom, where it is loud and busy. He sits with his friends and eats, singing, “I’m eating in my school shoes!” After that, Pete and his friends play outside on the playground with swings and tall slides. Pete slides and swings and sings, “I’m playing in my school shoes!” Later, Pete also sings about painting, heading, and riding. When school ends, he rides the bus home and tells his mom about his day.

summaries.summary: Duncan went to his room and found a pile of letters on his desk. The letters were from his crayons. Red crayon said he worked too hard coloring fire, jeans, apples, strawberries, and holiday pictures. Purple crayon said Duncan used too much color outside the lines. Beige crayon said he was tired of being called light brown or dark tan, and he wanted to color more than wheat and turkey dinners. Gray crayon said big animals like elephants, rhinos, and hippos made him very tired, and he wished for smaller things sometimes. White crayon said he was hard to see because he only colored snow or empty spaces. Black crayon said he was tired of making outlines for other colors. Green crayon said he liked his work, but yellow and orange were arguing about who was the color of the sun. Yellow said he was used for the sun in a farm book. Orange said he was the sun color too, and he pointed to zoo pages. Blue said he was short and stubby from coloring oceans, lakes, rivers, rain, and sky. Pink said Duncan had not used him in a year. Peach said Duncan peeled off his paper and left him naked. Duncan read all the letters and learned each crayon had something to say.

summaries.summary: Pete the Cat is eating a banana. He likes bananas because they are sweet, tasty, and easy to peel. He puts a banana in his cereal and on his peanut butter sandwich. Then Pete eats a bad banana. It is mushy and yucky, and his tummy hurts. Pete tells his mom he will not eat bananas again. His mom tries to help by making banana bread, banana cream pie, and a banana split, but Pete says no to all of them. Pete then tries other foods. He tastes a lemon, a pickle, an orange, fish, plums, rice, hot dogs, watermelon, and nut bread. Later, it is time for the big race. Pete thinks about breakfast and decides he wants a banana again. Greg the monkey gives him another banana. Pete peels it, takes a small bite, and sees it is good. Pete wins the race and thanks Greg. Pete is bananas for bananas.

summaries.summary: Long ago in a twinkling forest, Skellyy the skeleton lived with three witch friends named Willow, Hazel, and Tany. Willow brewed starry tea, Hazel danced with fireflies, and Tany knitted spells into scarves. Skellyy loved their walks and their music. One night he came to the cottage with big news. The moonlight feast was tomorrow, and he would bring dessert. He said he would make bone berry pie and pick the berries that night in the whispering woods. The witches were happy, but they also warned him that the woods could be tricky after dark. Skellyy went off at once, humming his bone-rattling tune. In the woods, he searched for the berries, but a bush puffed pink smoke in his face. He sneezed, spun around, and got lost. When the witches saw he was gone too long, Tany got her moon map and they called Greta. They flew out together, found Skellyy, and took him home. That night they made moonberry muffins and laughed under the glowing moon.

summaries.summary: Johnny Appleseed was the name people used for John Chapman, a gentle man who planted apple trees on the American frontier. The story starts when young Hannah Goodwin sees him at her family’s house. He is barefoot, thin, and wearing old clothes. The Goodwins welcome him in for food and talk. Johnny says he cannot stay because he must travel on and plant apple trees across the Great Frontier. He speaks about the wild land, the pioneers, and how apple trees will help the country grow. He carries a sack of seeds and a Bible, and he says he will not use a gun or knife. Hannah grows up hearing stories about his long journeys through bad weather and lonely places. She hears that he planted seeds, loved the forest and its animals, and was trusted by the Indians. In the end, old Hannah sees Johnny again near her orchard.
